name: Rear-door heat exchangers
applications: Racks of 20-80 kW where liquid cooling is not yet installed
principle: A rear-door heat exchanger replaces the rack's rear door with a liquid coil. Server fans push exhaust air through the coil, so heat leaves in water rather than in room air. Passive units rely entirely on server fans; active units add variable-speed fans. The coil handles the rack's heat at its own density, which is why the door approach reaches densities room air cooling cannot.

process_steps.name: Server fans discharge hot air at the rack rear
Door coil absorbs the heat into facility or local water
Water loop carries heat to the cooling plant
Cooled air returns to the room or directly to the cold aisle

key_equipment: active rear-door units with variable-speed fans
modulating valves and return-water temperature control

performance.metric: supported rack density, rear-door heat exchanger
performance.basis: Vertiv article: rear-door heat exchangers support rack densities from 20 to 80 kW, against a practical air-cooling limit of around 20 kW.

source.note: Vertiv, How rear door heat exchangers (RDHx) support high-density rack cooling, read 2026-11-14

advantages: Reaches 20-80 kW per rack without changing the room architecture
Rack-agnostic and deployable without facility water
Can be installed incrementally, rack by rack
limitations: Puts water at the back of the rack, so leak response matters
Passive units depend on server fan head and can constrain airflow
Return-water temperature control adds a control loop to commission
